This page puts the whole site together in one small study, from the messy abstraction workbook to the Methods and Results of a manuscript. Steps 1 to 7 do the work, in R and Python. Step 8 is the manuscript itself, and it's also a Word document: **MS Word**, under "Other Formats" in the right margin. The Word file contains only the manuscript, built from the same code every time the site is rendered.

::: {.callout-note .page-brief}
## 🎯 Goals and time
**After this page you can:**

- Write a manuscript's Methods and Results from your own analysis code, with each group's numbers, every estimate's 95% CI and the p-value, as step 8 does.
- Run the checks a reviewer may ask for on a primary result: a rank-based test when many patients score the maximum, and a regression that adjusts for the pre-op score.
- Spot the patients a complete-case analysis leaves out, and test whether they were left out more often after one procedure than after the other.

**Time:** about 45 minutes to read, about 2.5 hours with the exercises (an estimate).

**Read first:** [page 1](../foundations/01-tidy-data.qmd) on tidying the workbook, [page 2](../foundations/02-demographics.qmd) on Table 1 and SMDs, [page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd) on judging a distribution, [page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd) on Welch's t test, [page 12](../catalog/12-predict-from-several.qmd) on multiple linear regression and [page 13](../survival/13-kaplan-meier.qmd) on competing risks: the steps build on them.
:::

## 1 · The research question {#question}

Write the question down before you look at the [outcome](../glossary.qmd#outcome){.term} data, together with the [primary outcome](../glossary.qmd#primary-outcome){.term} and the analysis that will answer it. Deciding these after seeing the results makes any [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} meaningless ([page 15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#planned-comparisons)). For this study:

- **Question:** do patients improve as much in the first year after a total knee replacement (TKA) as after a total hip replacement (THA)?
- **Primary outcome:** the change in the joint-specific score from before surgery to 1 year: HOOS JR after THA, KOOS JR after TKA, each scored 0 to 100, higher is better.
- **Primary analysis:** the difference in [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} change between THA and TKA, with its 95% [CI](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term}, from [Welch's t test](../glossary.qmd#welch-test){.term} ([page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t)), if the changes look roughly [symmetric](../glossary.qmd#symmetric){.term} within each group ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd)). Otherwise the [Mann-Whitney test](../glossary.qmd#mann-whitney-test){.term}.
- **Secondary outcome:** revision of any component, as a [cumulative incidence](../glossary.qmd#cumulative-incidence){.term} with death as a [competing risk](../glossary.qmd#competing-risk){.term} ([page 13](../survival/13-kaplan-meier.qmd#competing-risks)).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: two questionnaires
HOOS JR and KOOS JR are different questionnaires. Both run from 0 to 100, but a 10-point gain on one isn't guaranteed to mean the same as a 10-point gain on the other. The comparison is still common in the literature, but say plainly in the Methods that it compares points on each joint's own scale. A stronger design uses a score every patient completes, such as PROMIS-29+2 physical function.
:::

## 2 · Tidy the raw workbook {#tidy}

The data come from the abstraction workbook that [page 1](../foundations/01-tidy-data.qmd#tidying) tidies step by step: 60 cases from each site, with banner rows, merged headers, mixed dates, five spellings of "missing" (`N/A`, `unk`, `-`, `999` and empty cells) and revisions marked only by a red fill. The code below is page 1's five steps in one block; open it to see the code, and go back to page 1 for why each step is there.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="The tidying code from page 1"}
# Step 1: read both tabs as text; the group header says pre-op first, then 1 year
read_site <- function(sheet) {
  raw <- read_excel(path, sheet = sheet, skip = 3, col_types = "text", .name_repair = "minimal")
  names(raw) <- str_trim(names(raw))
  names(raw)[names(raw) == "Date"]  <- c("prom_preop_date", "prom_1yr_date")
  names(raw)[names(raw) == "Score"] <- c("prom_preop", "prom_1yr")
  raw |>
    janitor::clean_names() |>
    mutate(site = sheet)
}
raw <- bind_rows(read_site("Site A"), read_site("Site B"))   # stack the tabs by column name

# Steps 2 and 3: drop the totals rows, duplicates and identifiers; one way to say "missing"
missing_codes <- c("N/A", "unk", "-", "999")
step3 <- raw |>
  filter(is.na(pt_name) | pt_name != "TOTAL") |>
  distinct() |>
  select(-pt_name, -mrn, -mua) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) if_else(x %in% missing_codes, NA, x)))

# Step 4: revisions are marked only by a red fill on the Study ID cell
cells <- xlsx_cells(path)
fills <- xlsx_formats(path)$local$fill$patternFill$fgColor$rgb
revised_ids <- cells |>
  filter(fills[local_format_id] %in% "FFFF9999") |>
  pull(character) |>
  str_trim() |>
  unique()

# Step 5: give every column its real type
parse_messy_date <- function(x, day_first = TRUE) {
  serial <- !is.na(x) & str_detect(x, "^\\d{5}$")
  iso    <- !is.na(x) & str_detect(x, "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$")
  rest   <- !is.na(x) & !serial & !iso
  out <- as.Date(rep(NA, length(x)))
  out[serial] <- janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(as.numeric(x[serial]))
  out[iso]    <- ymd(x[iso])
  out[rest]   <- if (day_first) dmy(x[rest], quiet = TRUE) else mdy(x[rest], quiet = TRUE)
  out
}

tidy <- step3 |>
  rename(procedure_text = procedure) |>
  transmute(
    case_id      = str_trim(study_id),
    site,
    surgery_date = parse_messy_date(dos),
    age          = parse_number(age),
    sex          = case_when(str_to_lower(sex) %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female",
                             str_to_lower(sex) %in% c("m", "male")   ~ "Male"),     # anything else -> NA
    bmi          = parse_number(bmi),
    asa          = as.integer(as.roman(str_remove(asa, "^ASA "))),
    diabetes     = as.integer(str_detect(comorbidities, regex("\\bDM\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))),
    hypertension = as.integer(str_detect(comorbidities, regex("\\bHTN\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))),
    sleep_apnea  = as.integer(str_detect(comorbidities, regex("\\bOSA\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))),
    procedure    = case_when(str_detect(procedure_text, regex("TKA|knee", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "TKA",
                             str_detect(procedure_text, regex("THA|hip", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "THA"),
    side         = case_when(str_detect(procedure_text, "\\b(L|Left)\\b") ~ "L",
                             str_detect(procedure_text, "\\b(R|Right)\\b") ~ "R"),
    los_days     = parse_number(los),
    revised      = as.integer(case_id %in% revised_ids),
    prom_preop_date = parse_messy_date(prom_preop_date),
    prom_preop      = parse_number(prom_preop),
    prom_1yr_date   = parse_messy_date(prom_1yr_date),
    prom_1yr        = parse_number(prom_1yr)
  ) |>
  arrange(site, case_id)

dim(tidy)

```{.python .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="The tidying code from page 1"}
# Step 1: read both tabs as text; pandas names the repeated headers "Date.1" and "Score.1"
def read_site(sheet):
    raw = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=sheet, header=3, dtype=str)
    names = [str(c).strip() for c in raw.columns]
    pairs = {"Date": "prom_preop_date", "Score": "prom_preop",
             "Date.1": "prom_1yr_date", "Score.1": "prom_1yr"}
    names = [pairs.get(n, n) for n in names]
    raw.columns = [re.sub(r"[^0-9a-z]+", "_", n.lower()).strip("_") for n in names]
    return raw.assign(site=sheet)

raw = pd.concat([read_site("Site A"), read_site("Site B")], ignore_index=True)   # stack by column name

# Steps 2 and 3: drop the totals rows, duplicates and identifiers; one way to say "missing"
step3 = (raw[raw["pt_name"] != "TOTAL"]
         .drop_duplicates()
         .drop(columns=["pt_name", "mrn", "mua"])
         .replace(["N/A", "unk", "-", "999"], pd.NA))

# Step 4: revisions are marked only by a red fill on the Study ID cell
revised_ids = set()
for sheet in openpyxl.load_workbook(path).worksheets:
    for row in sheet.iter_rows(min_row=5):
        for cell in row:
            if cell.fill.fgColor.rgb == "FFFF9999":
                revised_ids.add(str(cell.value).strip())

# Step 5: give every column its real type
def number(text):
    return pd.to_numeric(text.str.extract(r"(\d+\.?\d*)")[0])

def parse_messy_date(col, dayfirst=True):
    iso = col.str.match(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", na=False)
    swiss = col.notna() & ~iso
    dates = pd.concat([pd.to_datetime(col[iso], format="ISO8601"),
                       pd.to_datetime(col[swiss], format="mixed", dayfirst=dayfirst)])
    return dates.reindex(col.index)

asa_roman = {"I": "1", "II": "2", "III": "3", "IV": "4"}
procedure_text = step3["procedure"]

tidy = pd.DataFrame({
    "case_id":      step3["study_id"].str.strip(),
    "site":         step3["site"],
    "surgery_date": parse_messy_date(step3["dos"]),
    "age":          number(step3["age"]),
    "sex":          step3["sex"].str.lower().map({"f": "Female", "female": "Female",
                                              "m": "Male", "male": "Male"}),   # anything else -> missing
    "bmi":          number(step3["bmi"]),
    "asa":          pd.to_numeric(step3["asa"].str.replace("ASA ", "").replace(asa_roman)),
    "diabetes":     step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bDM\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "hypertension": step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bHTN\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "sleep_apnea":  step3["comorbidities"].str.contains(r"\bOSA\b", case=False).astype(int),
    "procedure":    np.select([procedure_text.str.contains(r"TKA|knee", case=False),
                               procedure_text.str.contains(r"THA|hip", case=False)],
                              ["TKA", "THA"], default=None),
    "side":         np.select([procedure_text.str.contains(r"\b(?:L|Left)\b"),
                               procedure_text.str.contains(r"\b(?:R|Right)\b")],
                              ["L", "R"], default=None),
    "los_days":     number(step3["los"]),
    "revised":      step3["study_id"].str.strip().isin(revised_ids).astype(int),
    "prom_preop_date": parse_messy_date(step3["prom_preop_date"]),
    "prom_preop":      number(step3["prom_preop"]),
    "prom_1yr_date":   parse_messy_date(step3["prom_1yr_date"]),
    "prom_1yr":        number(step3["prom_1yr"]),
}).sort_values(["site", "case_id"]).reset_index(drop=True)

print(tidy.shape)

assert (study["procedure"] == study["procedure_registry"]).all() and (study["revised"] == study["revised_registry"]).all()

Every check passed, so the code ran on. The workbook agrees with the [registry](../glossary.qmd#registry){.term} on the surgery date, the procedure and the revisions for all 120 cases. Checking one source against another catches what neither can alone: a red fill the abstractor forgot, or a study ID linked to the wrong registry record. The registry also shows that the 120 cases are 120 different patients, so each row is one patient. The last output counts the [missing values](../glossary.qmd#missing-data){.term}: 8 BMIs, 3 ASA classes, 3 lengths of stay, 5 pre-op scores and 22 one-year scores. The workbook can't tell why a value is missing: a value the abstractor couldn't find and a visit the patient never came to are both written as one of the five spellings of "missing" (step 2). For the 1-year scores the registry can say more, and the analysis has to say how it handles them.

### Who has no 1-year score? {#missing-scores}

The workbook can't say why a score is missing, but the registry shows what happened to every patient in the first year after surgery. Cross-tabulate the two: which scores each patient has, against whether the patient was revised, died or was [censored](../glossary.qmd#censored){.term} before 1 year.

                            is.na(prom_preop) ~ "no pre-op score",

         before_1_year = factor(before_1_year, levels = c("revised", "died", "censored", "still followed")))

All 5 without a pre-op score were still followed at 1 year. Of the 22 without a 1-year score, 7 were followed in the registry for less than 1 year, as the second output shows: 4 were revised (at 0.19, 0.26, 0.45 and 0.81 years), 1 died (at 0.93 years), and 2 had been censored (registry follow-up of 0.04 and 0.16 years) with neither a revision nor a death. The other 15 were still followed at 1 year, and the data don't say why their score is missing.

This changes how to read the result. The primary analysis (step 6) compares the change in patients with both scores, and a patient revised or dead in the first year has no 1-year score, so every early failure is left out of it. Its result describes the improvement of patients whose joint was still in place, and who were still followed, at 1 year; the revisions are counted in step 7 instead. The Methods say so, and the Results give the counts. Exercise 3 asks whether the scores were missing more often after one procedure than after the other.

## 🔀 R vs Python: SMDs
The SMDs agree to two decimals. The two packages also subtract the groups in opposite orders, so their signs differ: the R table shows absolute values, as page 2 advises, and tableone's keep their signs. The layouts differ too. gtsummary adds a Missing row with a count for each group; tableone has a Missing column with the total (BMI: 4 + 4 = 8). For a [yes/no](../glossary.qmd#binary){.term} variable, gtsummary shows one row, for "yes"; tableone shows a row for 0 and a row for 1.

Reading it:

R prints the two means under `sample estimates` but not their difference: 42.42 − 33.40 = 9.02. Python prints it on the `difference =` line. R's CI is under `95 percent confidence interval`. As a [rough guide](../glossary.qmd#cohen-benchmarks){.term}, 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large ([page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t)). So 0.66 is medium-to-large at the [point estimate](../glossary.qmd#estimate){.term}, but the CI runs from a small difference to a large one.

## 🔀 R vs Python: Hedges' g
Hedges' g is [Cohen's d](../glossary.qmd#cohens-d){.term} shrunk slightly to correct for small [samples](../glossary.qmd#sample){.term}. effectsize uses the exact correction, pingouin a close [approximation](../glossary.qmd#exact-test){.term}, so with 93 patients they differ in the sixth decimal: 0.664922 in R, which prints it rounded as 0.66, and 0.664925 in Python. For the CI, pingouin's `compute_esci()` uses an approximate formula and rounds to 2 decimals, so its CI, 0.24 to 1.09, is slightly wider than effectsize's 0.25 to 1.08, which comes from the noncentral t distribution. Say which you used; the manuscript quotes R's.
:::

### A sensitivity analysis: adjusting for sex {#sensitivity}

[Table 1](../glossary.qmd#table-1){.term} showed that the groups differ most in sex: 71.7% of the THA patients were women against 49.3% of the TKA patients (step 4). If women and men improve by different amounts, part of the 9-point difference could come from the different mix of sexes, not from the procedure. A [sensitivity analysis](../glossary.qmd#sensitivity-analysis){.term} checks this: a [linear regression](../glossary.qmd#linear-regression){.term} of the change on the procedure and sex gives the difference between procedures for patients of the same sex ([page 12](../catalog/12-predict-from-several.qmd#multiple-linear-regression)). It [adjusts](../glossary.qmd#adjustment){.term} for sex alone, because sex is the largest difference in Table 1 and no patient's sex is missing, so all 93 patients stay in the model. The pre-op score, the other difference that matters for a change, is exercise 2's question. This adjustment was not in step 1's plan: it was chosen after Table 1 showed the difference, while a real protocol names the variables it will adjust for in advance ([page 12](../catalog/12-predict-from-several.qmd#multiple-linear-regression)). So the Methods label it [post hoc](../glossary.qmd#post-hoc-test){.term}, which here means unplanned, not the pairwise post-hoc tests of [page 15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd): it is an [exploratory analysis](../glossary.qmd#prespecified){.term}, chosen after looking at the data, and its result suggests questions for later studies. The primary analysis stays the one step 1 planned.

## 7 · Revision: a survival analysis {#survival}

The secondary [outcome](../glossary.qmd#outcome){.term} is revision. First, how long were patients [followed](../glossary.qmd#follow-up){.term}? The [reverse Kaplan-Meier method](../glossary.qmd#reverse-kaplan-meier){.term} answers that: it treats the end of follow-up as the [event](../glossary.qmd#event){.term}, and revisions and deaths as [censored](../glossary.qmd#censored){.term} (`event_status == 0` in the code; [page 13](../survival/13-kaplan-meier.qmd#follow-up)). Then, what [proportion](../glossary.qmd#proportion){.term} were revised over time? 18 patients died during follow-up without a revision, so death is a [competing risk](../glossary.qmd#competing-risk){.term}: the [cumulative incidence](../glossary.qmd#cumulative-incidence){.term} gives the real proportion revised, where 1 − [Kaplan-Meier](../glossary.qmd#kaplan-meier){.term} would overstate it ([page 13](../survival/13-kaplan-meier.qmd#competing-risks)). Its [estimator](../glossary.qmd#estimate){.term} is called [Aalen-Johansen](../glossary.qmd#aalen-johansen){.term}, the name the Methods use; `survfit()` and `CumIncidenceRight()` both compute it.

## Aim {#aim}

To compare the improvement in joint-specific patient-reported scores from before surgery to 1 year after primary total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA), and to describe the cumulative incidence of revision.

## Methods {#methods}

**Patients and data.** This cohort study included 120 primary THAs and TKAs performed at two sites (60 at each) between January 2015 and November 2024, in 120 patients (one joint per patient). Patients' characteristics, the procedure and patient-reported scores were abstracted from the medical record into a standard sheet. Follow-up for revision and death came from the joint registry, linked by study ID.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was the change in the joint-specific score from before surgery to 1 year: the HOOS JR after THA and the KOOS JR after TKA, each scored from 0 to 100 (higher is better). The assessment windows were 0 to 30 days before surgery for the pre-op score and 300 to 425 days after surgery for the 1-year score; every recorded score fell inside them. Because the two are different instruments, the comparison is of points on each joint's own scale. The secondary outcome was revision of any component.

**Statistical analysis.** The primary outcome and the primary analysis were specified before the outcome data were examined. Continuous variables are reported as mean (SD) and categorical variables as n (%); differences between procedures at baseline are described with standardized mean differences. The change in score was compared between procedures with Welch's t test in patients with both scores (complete-case analysis), and summarized as the mean difference with its 95% CI and Hedges' g. Patients who were revised or died before 1 year had no 1-year score and were therefore not in this analysis. In a post hoc sensitivity analysis, the difference in the change in score was adjusted for sex, the largest baseline difference (@tbl-baseline), by linear regression. For revision, time was measured from the date of surgery to revision, death without revision (a competing event) or the end of registry follow-up (censored). Median follow-up was estimated with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method, censoring revisions and deaths. The cumulative incidence of revision was estimated with the Aalen-Johansen method, treating death as a competing risk. Tests were two-sided. Analyses used R 4.6.0 with the packages gtsummary 2.6.1 and smd 0.8.0 (Table 1), effectsize 1.0.3 (Hedges' g), survival 3.8-12 (follow-up and cumulative incidence) and ggsurvfit 1.2.1 (Figure 1).

## Results {#results}

Of the 120 patients, 53 (44.2%) had a THA and 67 (55.8%) a TKA (@tbl-baseline). Women made up 38 of 53 THA patients (71.7%) and 33 of 67 TKA patients (49.3%; SMD 0.47). The mean pre-op score was 48.1 points (SD 11.5) in THA patients and 51.0 points (SD 11.8) in TKA patients (SMD 0.26).

Both scores were available for 93 patients (77.5%): 46 of 53 after THA (86.8%) and 47 of 67 after TKA (70.1%). Of the other 27, 5 had no pre-op score (all after TKA) and 22 had no 1-year score; before 1 year, 4 of the 22 had been revised, 1 had died and 2 had been censored (registry follow-up of 0.04 and 0.16 years), and 15 were still followed. The mean change in score was 42.4 points (SD 13.0) after THA and 33.4 points (SD 13.9) after TKA (difference 9.0 points, 95% CI 3.5 to 14.6; Hedges' g 0.66, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.08; p = 0.002). Adjusted for sex, the difference (THA minus TKA) was 9.3 points (95% CI 3.5 to 15.0; p = 0.002). At 1 year, 15 of 46 THA patients (32.6%) and 7 of 47 TKA patients (14.9%) had the maximum score.

Over a median follow-up of 6.05 years (IQR 4.16 to 8.27), 18 patients had a revision and 18 died without one. The cumulative incidence of revision was 3.4% (95% CI 1.1% to 7.8%) at 2 years and 12.6% (95% CI 7.0% to 19.8%) at 5 years (@fig-revision).

## 📌 Key points
- Write down the question, the primary outcome and the analysis before you look at the outcome data: deciding them after seeing the results makes any p-value meaningless.
- Write each check of the tidy data so that it stops the script when it fails: a check that only prints something is easy to scroll past.
- In an observational study, Table 1 shows standardized mean differences instead of p-values: the question is how different the groups are, not whether the difference is "significant".
- HOOS JR and KOOS JR are different questionnaires, and a gain on one isn't guaranteed to mean the same as a gain on the other: say plainly in the Methods that the comparison is of points on each joint's own scale.
- A patient at the ceiling might have improved more if the scale allowed it, so when many patients score the maximum the improvement may be underestimated; a test that uses ranks instead of means checks the result (Exercise 1).
- Missing data are counted and reported, not dropped silently: the primary analysis compares patients with both scores, so every patient revised or dead in the first year is left out of it, and the Methods say so.
:::

**1.** Fifteen THA patients scored the maximum at 1 year. Check the primary result with a test that uses [ranks](../glossary.qmd#rank){.term} instead of [means](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term}: the [Mann-Whitney test](../glossary.qmd#mann-whitney-test){.term} and the [Hodges-Lehmann difference](../glossary.qmd#hodges-lehmann){.term} ([page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#mann-whitney)). Does the conclusion change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wilcox.test(change ~ procedure, data = analysed, exact = FALSE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

data:  change by procedure
W = 1461.5, p-value = 0.0035
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  3.600064 15.199914
sample estimates:
difference in location 
              9.499948 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
rank_check = stats.mannwhitneyu(tha, tka, alternative="two-sided", method="asymptotic", use_continuity=True)
print(rank_check.statistic, rank_check.pvalue)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
1461.5 0.0034996103353091236
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(np.median(np.subtract.outer(tha.to_numpy(), tka.to_numpy())))   # the Hodges-Lehmann difference
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
9.5
```


:::
:::

:::

> **Results:** The Hodges-Lehmann difference in the change was 9.5 points (95% CI 3.6 to 15.2; p = 0.003).

The conclusion doesn't change: 9.5 points is close to the 9.0 from the [t test](../glossary.qmd#t-test){.term}. Python gives the same [estimate](../glossary.qmd#estimate){.term} and [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}; its [CI](../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval){.term} needs a [bootstrap](../glossary.qmd#bootstrap){.term} ([page 6](../catalog/06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#mann-whitney)). R prints the p-value as 0.0035, which it has already rounded; Python shows 0.0034996, so to three decimals it is 0.003. In R, the estimate is on the `difference in location` line and its CI under `95 percent confidence interval`.

**2.** A reviewer writes: "TKA patients started with higher scores, so they had less room to improve. [Adjust for](../glossary.qmd#adjustment){.term} the pre-op score." Which analysis answers this, and what does it show?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

[Regress](../glossary.qmd#linear-regression){.term} the 1-year score on the procedure and the pre-op score ([page 12](../catalog/12-predict-from-several.qmd#multiple-linear-regression)). The procedure's [coefficient](../glossary.qmd#coefficient){.term} is the difference at 1 year between patients who started with the same score.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

::: {.cell}

summary(adjusted)$coefficients

The difference shrinks a little but doesn't go away, so the higher starting point explains only part of it.
